summary: For 8–9 year olds, build two linked ideas about evaporation and the water cycle: (1) the state changes — evaporation is liquid turning to invisible water vapour that mixes into the air (conserved, not destroyed or 'soaked in'), and condensation is water vapour cooling and turning back into liquid, for example on a cold surface or as tiny cloud droplets high in the air; and (2) the full cycle — the Sun evaporates water from seas, lakes, puddles, plants and ground; vapour rises, cools and condenses into clouds; water falls as precipitation; repeat, with water conserved throughout. Then investigate rate: warmer means faster evaporation when other conditions are kept the same, ideally shown by a controlled comparison. Directly confront two dominant misconceptions: water 'disappearing'/turning into air, and condensation having 'sweated through' a cold glass. Activities below span a manipulable model, a cold-glass close-up, a labelled diagram scaffold, a hands-on investigation, and recognition checks, each with a distinct pedagogical purpose.
misconceptions: Water in an open container is 'absorbed by the container', 'disappears', or 'turns into air' — rather than evaporating into invisible water vapour.
Condensation on a cold glass 'sweated' or 'seeped through' the container, instead of forming from water vapour in the surrounding air cooling on the surface.
Seeing the water cycle only as freezing and melting, missing evaporation and condensation (common for concrete thinkers).
Believing water only evaporates from seas/oceans, not from puddles, ground, plants and washing.
Failing to conserve water across the cycle — thinking water is created or lost rather than continuously recycled.

activities.title: Follow one tagged water drop around a manipulable cycle
steps: Tag one blob of water in a puddle, then step through the cycle watching the SAME tagged blob turn to invisible vapour, rise, cool into a cloud, and fall again as rain.
At each stage, name what is happening (evaporation, condensation, precipitation) and whether the water is liquid or gas.
State aloud whether any water was lost on the journey, and point to where the tagged blob is at each step.
Use a temperature control over a puddle or washing line: turn it up and watch the water shrink faster; turn it down and watch it barely budge.
In a controlled compare mode, set a warm dish beside a cool dish with equal water and everything else kept the same, then predict and watch which empties first.
activities.insight: Water is conserved as it cycles — the same water changes state and moves, it is never created or destroyed — and the rate of evaporation increases with temperature.

activities.title: Cold-glass close-up: where does the condensation come from?
steps: Look at droplets beading on the OUTSIDE of a cold glass or cola can.
Zoom in to watch water vapour particles arriving FROM the surrounding air and condensing onto the cold surface, shown with an arrow pointing from the air to the glass.
Explain in your own words why the drops are fresh water even when the drink inside is coloured.
Answer: did the water pass through the glass, or form from the air?
activities.insight: Condensation on a cold surface forms from water vapour already in the surrounding air cooling on the surface — it does not seep or sweat through the container.

activities.title: Labelled water-cycle diagram with reveal flaps (vocabulary scaffold)
steps: Tap each arrow/stage of a labelled cycle to hear evaporation, condensation, or precipitation and see the state change (liquid or gas).
Lift a flap on a cold glass that reveals: 'this water came from the air, not through the glass'.
Lift a flap that broadens evaporation sources beyond the sea to puddles, plants and washing.
Put the stages in order: evaporation, condensation, precipitation, collection.
activities.insight: The water cycle has named stages in a repeating loop, and evaporation happens from many sources (puddles, ground, plants, washing), not only the sea.

activities.title: Hands-on investigation: warm versus cool dish, with a covered dish and a sealed-bag mini cycle
steps: Put equal amounts of water in two identical dishes; place one on a warm sunny sill and one in a cool shady spot. The intended variable is warmth (note that the sunny spot is both warmer and brighter; for tighter control, pick two spots that differ mainly in warmth).

Optionally cover a third dish with cling film to trap any vapour, and/or set up a sealed-bag mini water cycle (a little water in a clear sealed bag taped to a sunny window) so you can watch water evaporate and re-condense inside with nothing escaping.
Before waiting, PREDICT which dish empties fastest, WHERE the water goes, and why.
After about a day, compare: note which dish lost most water, and look at the droplets on the covered lid or inside the sealed bag.

Record a puddle outline over hours (e.g. a playground puddle time series) and watch it shrink; link to everyday experience such as washing drying faster in the sun. (A snowman melting faster on a warm day is a different change, solid to liquid, so it is melting, not evaporation.)
Explain what the droplets on the covered lid or sealed bag show about where the water went.
activities.insight: Evaporation is faster when warmer, happens at everyday temperatures (not only boiling) from any exposed water, and the covered dish or sealed bag shows the water becomes vapour that is still there — it re-condenses rather than disappearing.

activities.title: Recognition checks on the key ideas
steps: Order the water-cycle stages into the correct sequence.
Match each process (evaporation, condensation) to its state change (liquid→gas, gas→liquid).
Answer a question on where condensation on a cold glass comes from (from the air, not through the glass).
Use a slider or choose an option to link higher temperature to faster evaporation.
activities.insight: Consolidate and self-check the vocabulary, sequence, condensation source, and rate relationship.

checkQuestion: Say: 'A puddle on the playground has disappeared by the afternoon on a hot day. Where did the water GO?' Then: 'Is it gone for good, or is it somewhere? How could that same water end up falling as rain?'
checkAnswer: The water evaporated — it turned into water vapour (an invisible gas) and spread into the air; it was not destroyed. The vapour rises, cools and condenses into cloud droplets, which fall as rain — the water cycle. It is the same water, conserved throughout.
